title: Blessed the womb (Luke 11:27–28)
hook: a woman praises his mother; he says blessed are they who hear the word and keep it; Catholics see Mary as both

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples asked to be taught to pray, and a man kept knocking at midnight. Your line was knock. Did you ask once more? Day four hundred sixty-two, the end of a week.

You've heard someone do this. A son gives a great speech at a wedding, and an aunt in the crowd calls out: your mother must be so proud! It's a compliment to him, routed through her. Something just like that happens in Luke. Jesus is in the middle of a tense argument with people who say he heals by the power of devils. He's answering them, and a woman in the crowd can't hold it in. She lifts up her voice and calls out a blessing on his mother. It's two verses long. Today, what she said, and what he said back.
screen: `YOUR MOTHER MUST BE SO PROUD.` → `A VOICE FROM THE CROWD.` → `TWO VERSES LONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the woman's cry in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the paps that gave thee suck." Paps is an old word for breasts. It's an earthy, motherly blessing, the kind women in that world gave: how happy the mother of such a son. And Jesus answers: "Yea rather, blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it." Some people hear that as a brush-off of his mother. Catholics hear something else, and Luke gives the reason. Go back to the beginning of this Gospel. When the angel came, Mary said be it done to me according to thy word. She heard the word and accepted it. At Bethlehem, Luke says, Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. When she visits Elizabeth, Elizabeth says blessed art thou that hast believed. And in her own song, Mary says all generations shall call me blessed. So in Luke, Mary is the woman from the crowd's blessing and the answer's blessing at once. She bore him, and she heard and kept the word. Augustine said it this way, in his own words: Mary was more blessed in receiving Christ by faith than in conceiving him in the flesh. Notice what that does. Jesus takes a blessing that only one woman in history could have, and opens it to everyone listening. Nobody else can be his mother. Anybody can hear and keep. Which is why Catholics honor Mary as the first disciple, not only as a mother: she shows what keeping looks like.
screen: `BLESSED IS THE WOMB THAT BORE THEE.` · `YEA RATHER: HEAR AND KEEP.` · `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.` · `ONE COULD BEAR HIM; ALL CAN KEEP.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY WHO HEAR AND KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one word today. Settle, and breathe. Think back over this week's lines: she loved much, nothing for the journey, no looking back, peace be to this house, knock. Let one of them choose you. Say it slowly inside a few times, the way Mary pondered. Don't analyze it. Just keep it, like a stone in your pocket you keep touching. If you pray, ask to keep it the way she did. The bell holds the time.
Blessed the womb. A woman's cry from the crowd praising Jesus' mother, and his answer: blessed are those who hear the word and keep it, as Mary did. Today's word.

Your line: hear and keep it. Carry your one word all day. And that's week sixty-six: she loved much, the women who funded him, take nothing, he set his face, the seventy-two, teach us to pray, and the womb. Day four hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics read Luke 11:27–28 on some feasts and Saturday Masses of Our Lady, and many pray the rosary as a way of pondering the Gospel's words with Mary.

fork.setup: a woman in the crowd calls out a blessing on your mother. how does Jesus answer?
options: say rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.
say his mother isn't to be praised.
fork.reveal: he widens the blessing to everyone who hears and keeps the word, and Luke has already shown Mary doing exactly that.

original.note: Greek: blessed, happy, the beatitude word. The woman uses it of the womb, and Jesus answers with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus brushed off a compliment to his mother.
what it means: he opens a blessing only Mary could have to everyone who hears and keeps the word, which Luke shows Mary doing too.
what a scholar hears: Luke uses keep (phylasso, and at Bethlehem syntereo) to tie Mary to the ideal hearer; menounge, yea rather, can mean yes, and even more.
